title: Personal guarantees: when the deal's debt becomes yours
summary: A personal guarantee is a promise that you will pay some or all of a project's loan if the project cannot. Knowing the type and the cap of each guarantee tells you exactly how much of your own wealth stands behind a deal.
body:
A personal guarantee turns part of a project's debt into your own debt if things go wrong. The two things to know about every guarantee are what triggers it and how much it is capped at.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, so far the capital stack has looked like a closed system: if the project fails, the losses stop at the equity you put in. A personal guarantee breaks that boundary. It is a separate promise, signed by a person, that the lender can enforce against that person's own assets.

Lenders ask for guarantees because development is risky and because they want the sponsor's full attention in a bad year. The main types, described in general terms, are:

  • Repayment guarantee. You promise to repay some or all of the loan. It may be full, or limited to a percentage, for example 25 percent of the loan, and it sometimes steps down as the project hits milestones.
  • Completion guarantee. You promise to finish construction and pay any cost overruns. Its size is open-ended, because it depends on what finishing costs.
  • Interest or carry guarantee. You promise to cover interest and operating shortfalls until the building is stabilized.
  • Carve-out guarantee, sometimes called a "bad boy" guarantee. The loan is otherwise non-recourse, but you become liable if specific acts occur, such as fraud, misapplying rent or filing for bankruptcy voluntarily.

For a capped repayment guarantee, the arithmetic is simple:

Guarantee cap (dollars) = loan (dollars) × guarantee percentage

Shortfall (dollars) = amount owed − what the lender recovers from the property

Guarantor pays = the smaller of (shortfall) and (cap)

A worked example

A hypothetical project has a 12 million dollar loan with a 25 percent repayment guarantee from the sponsor. The project fails and the lender sells the property for 9.5 million dollars. We ignore interest, legal costs and selling costs, all of which make real outcomes worse.

  1. Guarantee cap = 12 million × 0.25 = 3 million dollars.
  2. Shortfall = 12 − 9.5 = 2.5 million dollars.
  3. The guarantor pays the smaller of 2.5 million and 3 million, which is 2.5 million dollars, from personal assets.

Add that to the equity already lost in the project and the sponsor's total loss is the equity plus 2.5 million dollars. That is why a guarantee is often the largest single risk a developer carries: it is not visible in the project's numbers at all.

How lenders size up a guarantor

A guarantee is only worth what stands behind it, so lenders test the guarantor. A common approach, which varies by lender, is to ask for a net worth at least equal to the loan amount and liquidity, meaning cash and easily sold assets, of around 10 percent of the loan. These are market practice, not law. Lenders also add up every guarantee the person has signed on other deals, because one bad year can call several at once.

This lesson is conceptual. Whether a guarantee is enforceable, and how, depends on the documents and the jurisdiction, so any real guarantee should be reviewed with a lawyer. Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice.

Tonight's drill

Ignore interest, legal and selling costs.

Problem 1

A 20 million dollar loan carries a 20 percent repayment guarantee. What is the cap? What does the guarantor pay if the property sells for 17 million dollars? And if it sells for 14 million dollars, how much does the guarantor pay and how much does the lender lose?

Problem 2

A sponsor has a personal net worth of 6 million dollars, of which 1.5 million is liquid. They have already signed capped guarantees of 4, 3 and 2 million dollars on three deals. What are their total contingent guarantees as a share of net worth? A new lender proposes a 10 million dollar loan and uses the common tests of net worth at least equal to the loan and liquidity of at least 10 percent of the loan. Does the sponsor pass each test?

Problem 3

A lender offers a choice: a 25 percent repayment guarantee, or a completion guarantee only. What would you ask before choosing, and what would the lender be thinking?

The roommate question

Interconnected utilities can lean on each other in an emergency, but that also means a problem in one area can pull on another. How is a personal guarantee like an interconnection between a project and your personal balance sheet?

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Cap = 20 million × 0.20 = 4 million dollars.
  2. Sale at 17 million: shortfall = 3 million, below the cap, so the guarantor pays 3 million.
  3. Sale at 14 million: shortfall = 6 million, above the cap, so the guarantor pays 4 million and the lender loses the remaining 2 million.

The usual error: assuming a 20 percent guarantee means paying 20 percent of the shortfall. It means paying the shortfall up to a cap equal to 20 percent of the loan, so in a modest loss the guarantor can pay all of it.

Rule: the guarantor pays the shortfall, up to the cap.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Total contingent guarantees = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 million dollars, which is 9 ÷ 6 = 150 percent of net worth.
  2. Liquidity covers 1.5 ÷ 9 = about 17 percent of those guarantees.
  3. Net worth test: needs at least 10 million; has 6 million. Fails.
  4. Liquidity test: needs at least 1 million; has 1.5 million. Passes.

Even before the new loan, a bad year that called two of the existing guarantees could exceed the sponsor's liquid cash several times over.

The usual error: looking at each guarantee alone. Guarantees are contingent, so they are easy to ignore, but they are called in exactly the conditions when several deals struggle at once.

Rule: add up every guarantee you have signed, and compare the total with what you could actually pay.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
Questions to ask:

  • Does the repayment guarantee burn off? Many fall away or step down at completion or at a coverage milestone.
  • How firm is the construction price? With a fixed-price contract and a healthy contingency, a completion guarantee may carry less real risk than a repayment guarantee.
  • What sits in the carve-outs? Read which acts would turn a non-recourse loan into a full-recourse one.
  • What does it do to my other borrowing? Other lenders will count this guarantee against you.

The lender is thinking about which risk worries it most. A completion guarantee protects against the project being left half built, which is the worst outcome for a construction lender. A repayment guarantee protects against a fall in value after completion.

The usual error: choosing by the headline percentage. An uncapped completion guarantee can cost more than a capped repayment guarantee if construction goes badly.

Rule: judge a guarantee by its trigger and its cap, not its name.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
An interconnection lets neighbouring systems support each other, but it also creates a path for a disturbance in one area to draw on the other. A personal guarantee is that tie line between the project and your personal balance sheet: in normal times nothing flows across it, but when the project fails, the shortfall flows straight through to you. And just as interconnection limits are set to stop one area dragging the other down, a guarantee cap is the limit on how much the project can draw from you.

Rule: a guarantee is a tie line; know its limit before the disturbance.

rule: A personal guarantee makes part of the project's loss your own: know what triggers it, what it is capped at, and the total of every guarantee you have signed.

title: Concentration risk and holding company structures
summary: Too much of your wealth in one deal means one bad project can undo years of work. Holding each project in its own special purpose company can contain a failure, but only until a personal guarantee or a cross-default reaches past the wall.
body:
Concentration risk is how much of your wealth one deal can take with it. Separate companies for separate projects build walls between them, and personal guarantees are the doors through those walls.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, a developer can make every individual decision correctly and still be ruined by one project, simply because too much rode on it. That is concentration risk.

Concentration (percent) = your equity in one deal ÷ your total net worth × 100

If one deal is 50 percent of your net worth, then a total loss on that deal halves you, however good the others are. Many investors set a personal ceiling, for example no single deal above 20 to 30 percent of net worth. There is no correct figure; the point is to choose one deliberately.

Walls between projects

The structural tool is the special purpose vehicle, or SPV: a separate company that owns one project and nothing else. A common pattern, described here only in general terms, is:

  • Each project sits in its own SPV, which borrows its own loan.
  • A holding company owns the shares of the SPVs, and you own the holding company.
  • If one SPV fails, its lender's claim is generally limited to that SPV's own assets, especially on a non-recourse loan. The other SPVs are separate companies with separate creditors.

Lenders like SPVs too, because they want the project they lend on to be isolated from the developer's other troubles. That is why a lender often requires the borrower to be a new single-purpose company.

The walls have doors, and you must know where they are:

  • Personal guarantees reach past every company wall straight to you.
  • Cross-collateralization pledges one project's assets to support another's loan.
  • Cross-default clauses let a default on one loan count as a default on another.
  • Holding company guarantees put the holding company, and so every SPV it owns, behind one loan.
  • Mixing money between companies can weaken the separation that the structure relies on.

The tax treatment and the legal strength of any structure depend on the jurisdiction and the documents. This lesson is conceptual only: education, not financial, tax or legal advice. A real structure needs a lawyer and an accountant.

A worked example

A hypothetical sponsor has three projects with equity of 2, 3 and 5 million dollars, a total of 10 million dollars, and other assets of 2 million dollars, so a net worth of 12 million dollars. Project C is the largest, at 5 ÷ 12 = about 42 percent of net worth.

Project C fails. Its lender sells the property and is still owed 1.5 million dollars.

  1. Each project in its own SPV, non-recourse, no guarantee: the sponsor loses the 5 million dollars of equity in C. The lender's 1.5 million shortfall stays inside C's company. Net worth falls to 7 million dollars.
  2. Same structure, but a 25 percent repayment guarantee on C's 15 million dollar loan: the cap is 3.75 million, the shortfall of 1.5 million is below it, so the sponsor also pays 1.5 million personally. Net worth falls to 5.5 million dollars.
  3. All three projects in one company: the lender can generally claim against everything that company owns, so the 1.5 million shortfall is taken from A and B's value too. The sponsor loses 6.5 million dollars, and A and B now carry the scar of C's failure.

The walls changed how far the damage spread. But the deepest protection was not legal at all: it was not letting one project become 42 percent of everything.

Tonight's drill

Problem 1

A sponsor's net worth is 12 million dollars: 6 million in deal A, 3 million in deal B and 3 million in deal C. What is the concentration in A, and how much is lost if A goes to zero? If the sponsor caps any one deal at 30 percent, how much equity must come out of A, and what would a total loss on A then cost?

Problem 2

Projects A, B and C have equity of 4, 3 and 5 million dollars. B fails: its 3 million dollars of equity is lost and its lender is still owed 2 million dollars after selling the property. Compare the sponsor's total loss if all three projects are in one company, against each in its own SPV with a non-recourse loan and no guarantee. How much of A and C's equity survives in each case?

Problem 3

A lender on a new project asks to see your holding company structure. What would it ask, and which clauses would quietly undo the walls between your projects?

The roommate question

Grid operators separate systems into islands and protection zones so a fault is cleared without spreading. How is an SPV like a protection zone, and what plays the role of a breaker that fails to open?

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Concentration in A = 6 ÷ 12 = 50 percent. If A goes to zero, the sponsor loses 6 million, half of net worth.
  2. Cap at 30 percent: 0.30 × 12 million = 3.6 million in A, so 2.4 million must come out of A (assuming it can be sold or refinanced at its value, which keeps net worth at 12 million).
  3. A total loss on A would then cost 3.6 million, or 30 percent of net worth.

The usual error: judging a deal on its own return and ignoring its weight in your total. A good deal at 50 percent of net worth is still a 50 percent bet.

Rule: size each deal so that losing it is survivable.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. A and C together hold 4 + 5 = 9 million of equity.
  2. One company: B's lender can generally claim against the company's other assets. Loss = 3 million of B's equity + 2 million shortfall = 5 million. A and C keep 7 million of their 9 million.
  3. Separate SPVs, non-recourse, no guarantee: loss = B's 3 million of equity only. A and C keep all 9 million.
  4. If there had been a personal guarantee covering B's shortfall, the 2 million would come from the sponsor personally in either structure.

The usual error: assuming the SPV structure protects you from everything. It contains the shortfall, but B's own equity is lost either way, and a guarantee bypasses the wall entirely.

Rule: separate companies contain the shortfall, not the equity, and not the guarantee.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
Lender questions:

  • Is the borrower a new single-purpose company with no other assets, debts or history?
  • What other loans and guarantees exist at the holding company and personally?
  • Is anything cross-collateralized or cross-defaulted?
  • Who controls the holding company, and could a problem elsewhere change control of this project?

Clauses that undo the walls: personal or holding company guarantees, cross-collateralization, cross-default clauses, and carve-outs that make a non-recourse loan recourse. Also watch for practical breaches such as paying one project's bills from another's bank account.

The usual error: believing a structure chart is the protection. The documents signed on top of it decide whether the walls hold.

Rule: every guarantee and cross-clause is a door in the wall; count the doors.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
A protection zone is designed so that a fault inside it is cleared by its own breakers and the rest of the system keeps running. An SPV is the same idea: a failure inside one project is meant to be cleared inside that company. The breaker that fails to open is the guarantee or cross-default clause, because when it is present the fault is not cleared locally and instead propagates outward, to the holding company or to you personally. The structure only works if the boundaries actually isolate.

Rule: a wall that a guarantee runs through is not a wall.

rule: Keep any one deal small enough to lose, hold each project in its own company, and count every guarantee and cross-clause that reaches through the walls.

title: Mixed review: one deal, all six weeks
summary: This review runs one hypothetical deal through every tool in the course, from yield on cost and the pro forma to the capital stack, stress tests and guarantees. Each step feeds the next, which is how a lender or partner will actually read your numbers.
body:
Every week of this course was one lens on the same question: does this project make enough, and who is hurt if it does not? Tonight you run one deal through all six lenses in order.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, here is the whole course on one page:

  • Week 1, economics: yield on cost = NOI ÷ cost; value = NOI ÷ cap rate; spread = yield on cost minus cap rate; profit on cost = (value − cost) ÷ cost.
  • Week 2, profit versus cash: profit is earned on paper; cash goes out for months first, so the low point of cash, the cash valley, is what you must be able to fund.
  • Week 3, the pro forma: land, hard costs, soft costs, contingency and interest carry add up to total cost, and stabilized NOI only arrives after lease-up.
  • Week 4, the capital stack: loan-to-cost sets the equity; losses hit the top of the stack first.
  • Week 5, stress testing: DSCR = NOI ÷ debt service, and about 1.20x is a common lender minimum, not a law; test shocks together.
  • Week 6, personal protection: guarantees reach your own assets; concentration and structure decide how far a failure spreads.

A worked example

A hypothetical rental project.

  1. Pro forma. Land 3 million, hard costs 12 million, contingency at 10 percent of hard costs 1.2 million, soft costs 2.4 million, interest carry 1.4 million. Total cost = 3 + 12 + 1.2 + 2.4 + 1.4 = 20 million dollars.
  2. Economics. Stabilized NOI is 1.3 million dollars. Yield on cost = 1.3 ÷ 20 = 6.5 percent. At a 5.5 percent cap rate, value = 1.3 ÷ 0.055 = about 23.6 million. Profit = about 3.6 million, or about 18 percent on cost. Spread = 1.0 point.
  3. Capital stack. Senior loan at 60 percent loan-to-cost = 12 million, mezzanine 2 million, equity 6 million, which is 30 percent.
  4. Coverage. Both loans interest-only: senior at 6.5 percent costs 780 thousand a year, mezzanine at 12 percent costs 240 thousand, total 1.02 million. Senior DSCR = 1.3 ÷ 0.78 = about 1.67x. Combined DSCR = 1.3 ÷ 1.02 = about 1.27x.
  5. Stress. NOI falls 10 percent to 1.17 million: senior DSCR = 1.50x, still strong, but combined DSCR = 1.17 ÷ 1.02 = about 1.15x, below 1.20x. The mezzanine is where the pressure shows first.
  6. Loss order. If at the same time the market cap rate rises to 6.5 percent, value = 1.17 ÷ 0.065 = 18 million. Senior is paid 12, mezzanine 2, and the 6 million of equity gets 4 million back: a 2 million loss, a third of the equity, from a 10 percent fall in income.
  7. Cash and protection. That 3.6 million of profit does not exist in cash until sale or refinance. Meanwhile the equity went in first, and if the sponsor signed a guarantee, the loss could reach past the project to personal assets.

Notice how each lens changed the answer. The economics said 18 percent profit. The stress test said a modest miss breaks combined coverage. The loss order said that same miss costs the owners a third of their money. Only together do they describe the deal honestly.

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice.

Tonight's drill

One hypothetical deal across all three problems. Loans are interest-only; ignore fees and selling costs.

Problem 1

Weeks 1 and 3. Land 2 million, hard costs 8 million, soft costs at 20 percent of hard costs, contingency at 5 percent of hard costs, and interest carry of 1 million dollars. Stabilized NOI is 910 thousand dollars and the exit cap rate is 6 percent. Find total cost, yield on cost, value, profit on cost and the development spread. Then hard costs overrun by 10 percent and the contingency absorbs what it can: what is the new total cost and yield on cost?

Problem 2

Weeks 4 and 5. Using the original total cost from Problem 1, the senior loan is 70 percent loan-to-cost at 6 percent, and the rest is equity. Find the loan, the equity, the DSCR and the breakpoint NOI at 1.20x, and the percentage NOI can fall. Then, in a distressed sale for 10 million dollars, what does each layer get back and what percentage of equity is lost?

Problem 3

Weeks 2 and 6. The sponsor signed a 25 percent repayment guarantee on the Problem 2 loan. What is the cap, and what does the sponsor pay if the property sells for 7 million dollars? Then, as the lender, what would you ask the sponsor about cash and about their other deals, and why can a project showing profit still run out of cash?

The roommate question

Across six weeks you have met spreads, cushions, breakpoints, priority orders and isolation walls. Pick the one grid-reliability idea that best ties them together, and explain it in two sentences.

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Soft costs = 0.20 × 8 = 1.6 million. Contingency = 0.05 × 8 = 0.4 million.
  2. Total cost = 2 + 8 + 1.6 + 0.4 + 1.0 = 13 million dollars.
  3. Yield on cost = 0.91 ÷ 13 = 7.0 percent.
  4. Value = 0.91 ÷ 0.06 = about 15.17 million. Profit = about 2.17 million; profit on cost = 2.17 ÷ 13 = about 16.7 percent.
  5. Spread = 7.0 − 6.0 = 1.0 percentage point.
  6. Overrun = 0.10 × 8 = 0.8 million. Contingency absorbs 0.4 million, so total cost rises by 0.4 million to 13.4 million. Yield on cost = 0.91 ÷ 13.4 = about 6.79 percent.

The usual error: adding the whole overrun to total cost. The contingency was already in the budget, so only the overrun beyond it adds to cost.

Rule: contingency is spent before cost grows; only the excess moves the total.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Loan = 0.70 × 13 million = 9.1 million. Equity = 13 − 9.1 = 3.9 million.
  2. Debt service = 9.1 million × 0.06 = 546 thousand. DSCR = 910 ÷ 546 = about 1.67x.
  3. Breakpoint NOI = 1.20 × 546 thousand = 655.2 thousand. Room to fall = 254.8 thousand, and 254.8 ÷ 910 = 28 percent.
  4. Sale for 10 million: senior is paid 9.1 million in full; equity receives the remaining 0.9 million of its 3.9 million, a loss of 3.0 million, which is about 77 percent.

Check: total loss 3.0 million = cost 13 − proceeds 10. A 23 percent fall in value cost the owners 77 percent of their money.

The usual error: reading strong coverage, 1.67x, as safety for the equity. Coverage protects the lender's income; the equity is still first to lose when value falls.

Rule: coverage protects the loan; the cushion protects nothing above it.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
1. Cap = 0.25 × 9.1 million = 2.275 million dollars.
  2. Sale for 7 million: shortfall = 9.1 − 7 = 2.1 million, below the cap, so the sponsor pays 2.1 million personally, on top of losing all 3.9 million of equity.

Lender questions: how much liquid cash do you have against this guarantee? What other guarantees have you signed, and could they be called in the same downturn? Is this project a large share of your net worth? Who funds the cash valley if lease-up is slow?

Why profit is not cash: the 2.17 million of profit is only realized at sale or refinance. Before that, equity goes in first, interest is capitalized into the loan rather than paid from income, and months of lease-up pass before NOI reaches its stabilized level. A project can be profitable on paper and still need cash it does not have.

The usual error: treating the guarantee and the equity as separate risks. In a failure they are both called at once, so the real exposure is their sum: here 3.9 + 2.1 = 6.0 million.

Rule: your exposure to a deal is your equity plus every guarantee behind it.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
A good choice is operating margin against a defined limit. A development spread, an equity cushion, a 1.20x coverage line and a guarantee cap are all ways of measuring how far the deal can move before it hits a limit, exactly as a reliability coordinator watches the margin between flows and ratings. Priority orders and isolation walls then decide who absorbs the hit when the margin runs out, just as load-shedding schemes and protection zones do on the grid.

Rule: know your margin to every limit, and decide in advance who absorbs the breach.

rule: Read every deal through all six lenses: profit, cash, the pro forma, the stack, the stress test and your personal exposure.
